extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy; readers of Kant; philosophers
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and evaluation of Kant’s account of teleology, the moral argument for a final purpose and God, and the limits of theoretical proof versus practical faith; aimed at explicating what kinds of grounds and convictions are possible. Focuses on criteria for valid proofs, types of belief, and the regulative use of Ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final purpose must harmonize with moral purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: If the creation (the world) has a final purpose, we must think it as harmonising with the moral purpose (which alone makes the concept of a purpose possible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Idea of a final purpose of creation can only be sought in relation to rational beings; its objectivity cannot be given a priori by theoretical Reason but is grounded in practical Reason. The final purpose is a concept of practical Reason and cannot be inferred from experience for theoretical judging of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle for investigating nature: assume purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging in accordance with Reason, we have ground for assuming as a principle in the investigation of nature that nothing in nature is without a purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical Teleology exhibits abundant purposes in nature, and this assumption serves as a heuristic in investigating natural phenomena; nevertheless, the final purpose of nature as a whole is not produced by that investigation and must be sought in rational beings and practical Reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final purpose is a concept of practical Reason only
rubrics_metrics.description: A final purpose is merely a concept of our practical Reason, and can be inferred from no data of experience for the theoretical judging of nature, nor can it be applied to the cognition of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Its only legitimate use is for practical Reason according to moral laws: the final purpose of creation is that constitution of the world which harmonises with the final purpose of pure practical Reason insofar as that purpose is to be practical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral law supplies ground for possibility and practicability of final purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: In the moral law, which enjoins on us the application of our powers to the accomplishment of the final purpose, we have a ground for assuming its possibility and practicability, and consequently a nature of things harmonious with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because accomplishment might require concurrence of nature beyond our power, the moral law gives a moral ground for thinking a nature of things that cooperates with our moral purpose—hence a moral justification for assuming a final purpose of creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption of moral Being (God) is a practical/regulative postulate
rubrics_metrics.description: To account for creation in accordance with a final purpose we must assume not only an intelligent Being but a moral Being as author of the world (i.e. God), yet this conclusion holds merely for the Judgement according to concepts of practical Reason (reflective, not determinant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This does not determine anything theoretically about God's being; the idea is a practical-regulative principle that secures the practicability of the moral purpose for our will and conduct, not a theoretical proof of divine existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes of the supreme Being can only be thought analogically
rubrics_metrics.description: We can think the properties of the highest Being only according to analogy; we cannot thereby cognise Him or ascribe anything theoretically to Him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogical attribution is permissible as a regulative device to express our relation to the supersensible Being for practical purposes, but it must not be taken as constitutive knowledge of the Being’s inner constitution (avoid anthropomorphism and speculative claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit theoretical Reason to prevent theological errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitation of Reason in respect of Ideas of the supersensible has the use of preventing Theology from rising into Theosophy or into Demonology, and preventing Religion from turning into Theurgy or Idolatry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practical restriction protects religion and psychology from speculative overreach: do not use theoretical pretences about the supersensible to alter moral law or to found ethical precepts on questionable theological claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: A proof should convince, not merely persuade
rubrics_metrics.description: The first requisite for every proof is that it should not persuade but convince; the ground of proof or the conclusion should not be merely a subjective determining ground of assent (mere illusion), but objectively valid and a logical ground of cognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of natural-theological arguments that exploit human propensity to prefer unified explanations; eloquence and moral interest may persuade but do not substitute for objective logical force. The philosopher should expose persuasive illusions and distinguish persuasion from conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish physical teleology from moral teleology in argument
rubrics_metrics.description: The division of the proof into two dissimilar parts—belonging to physical and moral Teleology respectively—cannot and must not be prevented; blending these makes it impossible to discern where the proper force of the proof lies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the explanatory roles separate: physical teleology can indicate design-like regularities in nature, moral teleology concerns practical reasons for postulating final purposes. Conflation obscures which part (if any) has logical validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of theoretical grounds of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: All theoretical grounds of proof resolve themselves into: (1) logically strict Syllogisms of Reason; (2) Conclusions according to analogy; (3) Probable opinion; (4) Assumption of a merely possible ground of explanation (Hypothesis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each form has distinct epistemic weight and limits; when evaluating any putative proof one should identify which of these four forms it belongs to and apply the appropriate standards of rigor and possibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit of syllogistic (deductive) proofs for supersensible objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Logically accurate proofs (syllogisms from universal to particular) cannot establish a supersensible Being, because no intuition possible for us corresponds to the concept of a Being beyond nature; hence no ampliative theoretical cognition is possible about it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid attempting to deduce attributes of supersensible objects from principles valid only for sensible nature; deductive form alone cannot supply the missing empirical/material correlate required for cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy cannot transfer dissimilar specific determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: We can think one thing according to the analogy of another, but we cannot conclude from one to the other by analogy in respect of their dissimilarities—i.e., cannot transfer specific material determinations from natural causes to a supersensible original Being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogical reasoning may suggest a way of conceiving divine causality, but it cannot justify ascribing to the supreme Being the precise modes of causality known only in sensibly-conditioned beings (avoid illegitimate projection of human attributes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability has no place for a priori judgements about the supersensible
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinion finds no place in a priori judgements; empirical grounds cannot support probable opinions about what lies beyond experience, because probability presupposes a series of grounds susceptible of completion—impossible when part of the series lies outside possible experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat empirical teleological indications as yielding probabilistic support for supersensible claims; such 'probability' is illusory because the necessary completion of grounds cannot occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis demands certainty of possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If a hypothesis is to serve for the explanation of a phenomenon, at least its possibility must be completely certain; one cannot assume the possibility of a supersensible Being determined according to certain concepts without ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid adopting speculative hypotheses about supersensible beings unless their mere possibility can be shown free from doubt; otherwise one risks unfounded chimeras based only on the principle of contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: No theoretical proof of God or immortal soul is possible
rubrics_metrics.description: For the existence of the original Being (Godhead), or of the soul as an immortal spirit, absolutely no proof in a theoretical point of view is possible for human Reason that can bring about even the least degree of belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because we lack the necessary empirical/intuitive material to determine such Ideas theoretically, any claim to theoretical proof of these supersensible realities should be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three kinds of cognisable objects for 'what is for us'
rubrics_metrics.description: Cognisable things for us divide into: (1) things of opinion (opinabile); (2) things of fact (scibile); and (3) things of faith (mere credibile).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to classify claims: (1) opinable objects are empirically conceivable but not for us; (2) factual objects have objective reality provable by intuition or experience; (3) faith-objects are required by practical Reason and transcendent for theoretical cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Things of opinion belong to empirical possibility but not for us
rubrics_metrics.description: Things of opinion are always objects of an empirical cognition at least possible in itself but which, on account of our limited faculties, is for us impossible (e.g., ether, inhabitants of distant planets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such items as speculative but potentially decidable in principle by experience; they are not 'things of faith' and should not be elevated to moral postulates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Things of fact require objective reality via intuition or experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects whose objective reality can be proved (through pure Reason or experience and by means of a corresponding intuition) are things of fact (scibilia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical properties and empirical phenomena that can be presented in experience belong here; only these supply genuine theoretical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom as a special case: Idea that counts as a fact for practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The Idea of freedom, though transcendent theoretically, can be exhibited by means of practical laws and actual actions and consequently in experience; thus it is the only Idea of pure Reason that comes under things of fact for practical purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize freedom as uniquely positioned: it grounds moral responsibility and practical explanation even if it cannot be given a theoretical intuitive proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Things of faith are postulates of pure practical Reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects that must be thought a priori in reference to the use of pure practical Reason (but are transcendent for theoretical use)—the highest good, God, and immortality—are mere things of faith (res fidei).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such objects are assumed not on theoretical grounds but because practical Reason commands their assumption as conditions for the possibility of the moral final purpose; belief in them is moral faith adequate for practical ends but does not constitute theoretical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith (habitus) is a moral attitude distinct from opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Faith, as habitus not actus, is the moral attitude of Reason: a constant principle to assume as true what is necessary to presuppose as condition of the possibility of the highest moral final purpose though its possibility is inscrutable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faith is trust in the attainment of a design required by duty; it is a free moral belief grounded in practical Reason's demands and is neither mere credulity nor theoretical assent. Use faith to motivate moral action, not to claim speculative knowledge.
